title: QBR Metric Handbook — latency, uptime, cost-per-token, cache-hit (compact)
content:
Purpose:
A compact reference for Customer Success QBRs defining the canonical measurement, calculation, and interpretation for four core QBR metrics used in renewal conversations: latency, uptime, cost-per-token, and cache-hit rate. Meant as a one-page + annex that CS/AMs can copy into QBR decks and attach to renewal playbooks.

Audience:
Customer Success Managers, Solutions Engineers, Product Ops, and any stakeholder preparing QBRs for customers using Redwood Hosted / Dedicated / Private inference.

Quick notes on scope:
- Metrics are defined from the platform’s observability pipeline (ingested by Datadog/Prometheus -> normalized into the analytics warehouse). For Dedicated/Private customers we prefer host-reported metrics but fallback to agent-side metrics if absent.
- Reporting windows: QBRs typically use 90-day rolling windows with an optional 30-day lookback for recent trend lines.

Metric 1 — Latency (per-request tokenized latency)
Definition:
- Core metric: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end request latency measured in milliseconds (ms). End-to-end = request received by Redwood edge to final token emitted to client (streaming complete or non-streaming final token timestamp).
- Tokenized latency: when applicable, report both per-request latency and per-token generation latency (average time spent generating each produced token).

Measurement details / caveats:
- Use truncated traces to remove bot/healthcheck traffic. Exclude administrative/test API keys and synthetic load unless explicitly part of SLA testing.
- For streaming responses, latency for "first byte" (TTFB) and "completion" are separate. QBR summary should show: p95(TTFB), p95(completion).

Datadog example query (pseudo):
- p95_latency_ms = `p95(last_5m):trace.duration{env:prod,customer:ACME}.as_count()`
- per-token = `avg(token_generation_ms)` derived from server spans divided by output.token_count

Interpretation guidance for CS:
- Call out whether increases in high-percentile latency are correlated with request size (input length), model type, or recent routing changes.
- Suggested SLO bands (example): p50 < 100ms, p95 < 400ms, p99 < 800ms for chat-style workloads on Hosted standard tier. Adjust for larger models / long contexts.

Metric 2 — Uptime / Availability
Definition:
- Availability = fraction of successful requests over total requests (successful = HTTP 2xx or platform-specific success codes), measured over the reporting window. Expressed as a percentage.
- Complement with error-rate metrics: client-errors (4xx), server-errors (5xx), and timeouts (gated by the customer’s client timeout).

SLA vs observed metric:
- SLA example: 99.95% availability monthly for Dedicated customers. For Hosted customers we often reference platform-level SLA tiers.
- For QBRs, show both: rolling 90-day availability and outage incidents list (incidents with duration > 5 minutes).

Calculation (simple):
- availability_pct = 100 * (successful_requests / total_requests)

Incident callout table (text CSV):
- date, incident-id, duration-min, impact (pct-requests-affected), root-cause, mitigation
- 2024-11-03, INC-4321, 13, 8%, upstream-DB-throttle -> added burst capacity; permanent fix scheduled

Metric 3 — Cost-per-token (effective unit cost)
Definition:
- Effective cost-per-token is the effective infra/service cost attributed to tokens consumed by the customer. It’s a cost-accounting metric (not billed price). Useful for renewal conversations to justify SKU / capacity changes.

Basic formula (example):
- cost_per_token = (sum(infrastructure_costs_allocated_to_customer) + platform-overhead) / total_tokens_generated

Inputs and notes:
- Infrastructure costs include GPU hours, managed infra, storage for KV cache, network egress where billable, and reserved capacity amortization. For Hosted customers we use percent-of-virtual-usage model; for Dedicated we use committed-dollar amortization.
- Platform overhead = control plane, telemetry, and support costs allocated per customer or per cluster.

Sample spreadsheet row (CSV-like):
- month, infra_cost_usd, overhead_usd, total_tokens, cost_per_token_usd
- 2025-01, 14,320, 1,200, 48,500,000, 0.000320

Talking points for renewal:
- Show how batching, prefix-caching, or smaller quantized model variants can reduce cost_per_token by X%. Provide modeled scenarios (best, expected, conservative).

Metric 4 — Cache hit rate (KV / prefix / response cache)
Definition:
- Cache hit rate = cache_hits / (cache_hits + cache_misses) for the cache layer(s) relevant to the customer (prefix cache, KV cache, response cache). Expressed as a percent.
- Report by cache type when possible (prefix vs KV).

Why it matters:
- Higher cache hit rates reduce per-token compute and latency for repeated prompts (system prompts, reused prefix text). Cache effectiveness is a direct lever for unit-cost reduction and latency improvements.

Measurement guidance:
- Measure warm start vs cold start. For Dedicated customers with pinned models, warm caches will be higher. For Hosted multi-tenant workloads, hit rates will vary by traffic locality.

Sample metric breakdown (CSV-like):
- window, cache_type, hits, misses, hit_rate_pct
- 90d, prefix, 1,234,567, 987,654, 55.7%

KPI matrix (compact) — suggested QBR slide content (copyable)
- Column headers: metric, window, primary-stat, secondary-stat, target, recent-trend
- latency, 90d, p95=360ms, p99=720ms, target p95<400ms, trend=+12% vs prior 30d
- availability, 90d, 99.942%, incidents=2, target>=99.95%, trend=-0.01% vs prior 90d
- cost-per-token, 30d, $0.00033, 7-day-avg tokens=12.3M, target<=0.00030, trend=+8% (higher)
- cache-hit, 90d, 55.7%, prefix-hit=62% kv-hit=51%, target>=65% overall, trend=-3%

Annex — quick-run diagnostic checklist for CS before QBR
1) Query the last 90d latency p95/p99 and compare to the same prior window. Attach traces for top 3 offending request signatures.
2) Pull availability time-series and list any incidents affecting the customer (start/end + RCA link).
3) Produce cost-per-token breakdown: infra vs overhead vs networking. Run a model showing effect of a 10% cache-hit increase.
4) Check cache eviction logs for high churn namespaces; flag if eviction rate > 5% per hour.
5) Verify routing policies changed in the window (regions/model-fallback) and call out in QBR notes.

Common gotchas & recommended phrasing
- Don’t conflate billed price with effective cost. For negotiations, present both: billed spend vs normalized cost-per-token (transparency builds trust).
- If cache-hit drops after a release, note release-id and link to deployment PR and rollout notes.
- If latency worsens after a model change, show per-model p95 to isolate the regression.
